subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
skillName: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: This worksheet spans the whole cluster on random sampling. The first group of problems (7.SP.A.1) is about choosing and judging samples: telling a population from a sample, spotting bias, and deciding whether a sample is random and representative. The second group (7.SP.A.2) uses sample data to make estimates about a whole population and to gauge how much those estimates can vary.

items.prompt: A librarian wants to know the favorite genre of all $720$ students who use the school library. She surveys $60$ of them. Identify the population and the sample.
items.answer: Population: all $720$ students who use the library. Sample: the $60$ students she surveys.

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about. Here that is all $720$ students who use the library.
The sample is the smaller subset that is actually surveyed. Here that is the $60$ students.
So the population is all $720$ students and the sample is the $60$ surveyed students.

items.prompt: To pick a sample, a teacher writes every student's name on a slip, mixes the slips in a bag, and draws $25$ names without looking. Is this a random sample? Explain in one sentence.
items.answer: Yes, it is a random sample because every student has an equal chance of being drawn.

steps: A random sample gives every member of the population an equal chance of being selected.
Mixing all the name slips and drawing without looking gives each student the same chance of being chosen.
Therefore this is a random sample.

items.prompt: A reporter interviews the first $20$ people leaving a movie theater about the film they saw. Classify this sampling method as either a random sample or a convenience sample.

steps: A convenience sample chooses whoever is easiest to reach rather than selecting at random.
Interviewing the first people who happen to walk out is choosing the most available people, not a random draw.
So this is a convenience sample, not a random sample.

items.prompt: To learn how all residents of a city commute to work, a researcher surveys only people waiting at a downtown bus stop. Name the type of sampling and explain why the sample is biased.
items.answer: It is a convenience (location) sample, and it is biased because people at a bus stop are more likely to commute by bus, so they do not represent all commuters.

steps: The researcher surveys whoever is conveniently at one location, the bus stop, so this is a convenience sample with location bias.
People standing at a bus stop are far more likely to ride the bus than the average city resident.
This overrepresents bus riders and underrepresents people who drive, bike, or walk, so the sample does not mirror the whole population.
Because the sample is not representative, it is biased.

items.prompt: A radio station asks listeners to call in and vote on whether a new highway should be built. Identify this sampling method and explain one reason the results may be biased.
items.answer: It is a voluntary response sample, and it is biased because only listeners with strong opinions tend to call in, so they do not represent the whole population.

steps: When people choose whether to participate by calling in, the method is a voluntary response sample.
People who feel strongly, especially those who are upset or excited, are much more likely to take the time to call.
This self-selection means the callers are not representative of all listeners or residents.
Therefore the results are biased toward the opinions of those most motivated to respond.

items.prompt: A school of $600$ students wants opinions on a new dress code. Three plans are proposed: (a) survey the $15$ members of the basketball team, (b) draw $50$ student ID numbers from a hat and survey those students, (c) post an online form and use whoever chooses to respond. Which plan gives the most representative sample? Explain.
items.answer: Plan (b), drawing ID numbers from a hat, because it is a random sample that gives every student an equal chance of being chosen.

steps: Plan (a) surveys only athletes, a small unrepresentative subgroup, so it is biased.
Plan (c) is a voluntary response sample, so only students who choose to reply are heard, which is also biased.
Plan (b) draws ID numbers at random, giving every one of the $600$ students an equal chance of selection.
A random sample is most likely to mirror the whole student body, so plan (b) is the most representative.

items.prompt: A manager surveys $300$ of the company's $1200$ employees by standing in the cafeteria at noon and asking everyone who walks in. She says, "Because I surveyed so many people, my sample must be representative." Is her reasoning correct? Explain.
items.answer: No. A large sample does not fix bias. Surveying only people in the cafeteria at noon misses employees who eat elsewhere or work different shifts, so the sample is not representative.

steps: Whether a sample is representative depends on how it was chosen, not only on how big it is.
Standing in the cafeteria at noon is a convenience sample, so it overrepresents employees who eat there at that time.
Workers on other shifts or who eat elsewhere have little or no chance of being included, which biases the sample.
A large but biased sample is still biased, so her reasoning is incorrect.

items.prompt: From a random sample of $40$ of the $500$ books in a library, $10$ are mysteries. A student concludes that about $\frac{1}{4}$ of all the library's books are mysteries. Is this inference valid? Explain, and state what would make an inference like this untrustworthy.
items.answer: Yes, the inference is reasonable because the sample was random, so $\frac{10}{40}=\frac{1}{4}$ is a fair estimate. An inference like this would be untrustworthy if the sample had been biased (for example, taken only from the mystery shelf).

steps: The sample proportion of mysteries is $\frac{10}{40}=\frac{1}{4}$.
Because the $40$ books were chosen at random, the sample should reflect the whole collection, so estimating $\frac{1}{4}$ of all books is reasonable.
An estimate is only trustworthy when the sample is random and representative.
If the books had instead been pulled only from the mystery section, the sample would be biased and the $\frac{1}{4}$ estimate would not be valid, no matter how the math worked out.

items.prompt: In a random sample of $20$ of the $200$ students at a camp, $5$ chose swimming as their favorite activity. Estimate how many of all $200$ campers would choose swimming.

steps: Find the sample proportion who chose swimming: $\frac{5}{20}=\frac{1}{4}$.
Scale this proportion up to the whole population of $200$ campers: $\frac{1}{4}\times 200$.
So about $50$ campers would choose swimming.

items.prompt: A factory inspector checks a random sample of $50$ phone cases and finds $3$ are scratched. Estimate the percent of all the phone cases in the shipment that are scratched.

steps: Write the sample proportion of scratched cases: $\frac{3}{50}$.
Convert the fraction to a percent: $\frac{3}{50}=\frac{6}{100}=6\%$.
So about $6\%$ of all the phone cases in the shipment are estimated to be scratched.

items.prompt: In a random sample of $40$ students, $14$ said they walk to school. The school has $600$ students. Estimate how many students in the whole school walk to school.

steps: Find the sample proportion who walk: $\frac{14}{40}$.
Scale this proportion up to the population of $600$ students: $\frac{14}{40}\times 600$.
Compute: $\frac{14}{40}\times 600 = 14\times 15 = 210$.
So about $210$ students in the whole school walk to school.

items.prompt: A random sample of $80$ light bulbs from a large shipment contains $6$ defective bulbs. Estimate the percent of all bulbs in the shipment that are defective.

steps: Write the sample proportion of defective bulbs: $\frac{6}{80}$.
Convert to a percent by dividing: $\frac{6}{80}=0.075$.
So about $7.5\%$ of all the bulbs in the shipment are estimated to be defective.

items.prompt: Biologists catch a random sample of fish from a lake and find that $\frac{3}{20}$ of them are trout. They estimate the lake holds about $4000$ fish. About how many of the fish in the lake are trout?

steps: The sample proportion of trout is $\frac{3}{20}$.
Apply this proportion to the estimated population of $4000$ fish: $\frac{3}{20}\times 4000$.
Compute: $\frac{3}{20}\times 4000 = 3\times 200 = 600$.
So about $600$ of the fish in the lake are trout.

items.prompt: Four different random samples of $50$ voters each are taken. The percent favoring a ballot measure in the samples is $46\%$, $52\%$, $48\%$, and $50\%$. Use these results to give a single best estimate of the percent of all voters who favor the measure, and state a reasonable range for the true value.
items.answer: Best estimate: about $49\%$ (the average of the four samples). A reasonable range is $46\%$ to $52\%$.

steps: Average the four sample percents to get a single best estimate: $\frac{46+52+48+50}{4}=\frac{196}{4}=49\%$.
The four estimates spread from a low of $46\%$ to a high of $52\%$.
This spread shows how much same-size random samples vary, so the true value is likely somewhere in that band.
A reasonable range for the true percent is therefore $46\%$ to $52\%$, centered near $49\%$.

items.prompt: Two students estimate the percent of all $800$ students at a school who bring lunch from home. Ana takes a random sample of $50$ students and finds $20$ bring lunch. Ben surveys $120$ students by asking only people in the lunch line, and $84$ of them bring lunch. Use Ana's data to estimate the number of students who bring lunch, and explain whose estimate is more trustworthy.
items.answer: Ana's estimate is about $320$ students ($\frac{20}{50}\times 800$). Ana's estimate is more trustworthy because her sample was random, while Ben's larger sample is biased (people in the lunch line are less likely to have brought lunch from home).

steps: Use Ana's random sample proportion: $\frac{20}{50}=\frac{2}{5}$.
Scale up to the population of $800$ students: $\frac{2}{5}\times 800 = 320$ students.
Ben surveyed more people, but only students standing in the lunch line, who are less likely to have packed a lunch, so his sample is biased.
A larger sample does not fix bias; representativeness is what matters, so Ana's random estimate of about $320$ students is more trustworthy than Ben's.
